OSCAR PISTORIUS: THE STATE'S APPEAL AGAINST HIS SIX-YEAR SENTENCE

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Just more than a year and four months since Oscar Pistorius was sentenced to six years in prison for murder, his future hangs in the balance again.

Unique Selling Point:
In December 2015, Supreme Court of Appeal Justice Eric Leach, who wrote and read the ruling on behalf of a five-judge bench unanimous in its verdict, opened the verdict with the following words: "This case involves the human tragedy of Shakespearean proportions. The young man overcomes huge physical disabilities to reach Olympian heights as an athlete. He meets a young woman of great natural beauty and a successful model. All is destroyed when he takes her life. The court found the accused to have been a very poor witness. One does really not know what his explanation is having fired the fatal shots. I have no doubt that in firing the fatal shots the accused must have foreseen and therefore did foresee that whoever was behind the toilet door, might die, but reconciled himself to that event occurring and gambled with that person's life. He ought to have been convicted not of culpable homicide on that count, but of murder."

It is perhaps upon these words, that the NPA and the trial's chief state prosecutor, adv Gerrie Nel, said the sentence that Pretoria High Court Trial Judge, Thokozile Masipa, imposed on Oscar Pistorius on the charge of murder, is "shockingly inappropriate". And this is what the State will build its case on and argue in the Appeal Court in Bloemfontein on the 3rd of November.

In July 2016, when Judge Masipa sentenced Pistorius for a second time, she sentenced him to six years imprisonment for the murder of Reeva Steenkamp, saying the mitigating factors outweighed the aggravating factors and therefore the prescribed 15-year minimum sentence for murder would be unjust.

At the time, adv Nel said the sentence was too lenient and that the State would appeal it.
In August 2016, Judge Masipa dismissed the State's application for leave to appeal the sentence she imposed on Oscar. In dismissing the application, Judge Masipa said she was not persuaded that there was a reasonable prospect of success at another court.
Adv Nel then launched an application directly at the SCA, and in November last year the court ruled that the State and Defence would have to give oral arguments in the State's appeal against Oscar's sentence.

These are the arguments that will be heard on the 3rd of November in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein - and this appeal, once again, let Oscar Pistorius's future lies in the balance: another chapter of a protracted trial that has sustained global attention.



Summary:
In yet another chapter of the protracted court case - dubbed the "Trial of the Century" - that has sustained global interest, Oscar Pistorius's future again hangs in the balance.
It is the State's second appeal against the findings by Trial Judge Thokozila Masipa: first the successful appeal against the verdict of culpable homicide - overturned by the SCA in a unanimous judgment of a full bench of judges - to murder; and the State's second appeal against the six-year sentence Judge Masipa imposed on Pistorius for murder.
The State will argue that the former athlete's sentence is "shockingly inappropriate for the crime of murder". The NPA will argue that Pistorius should have been handed the minimum term of 15 years behind bars.
NPA spokesperson, Luvuyo Mfaku, said: "The State, in the papers, we stipulate that the sentence imposed is shockingly low. The presiding officer has the discretion to deviate from the minimum prescribed sentence when compelling and substantiate circumstances exist. But... with this matter, the presiding officer exercised that discretion in a very lenient manner."

Pistorius's defence team lead by defence advocate Barry Roux, has always argued that Pistorius did not deliberately kill Reeva Steenkamp. Pistorius has always insisted the shooting was a mistake, saying he thought an intruder had entered his home and he feared for his safety. He fired four shots through a locked toilet door, hitting Reeva in the head, arm and hip. During his trial in 2014, Pistorius testified in court it was only when he battered down the door with a cricket bat that he realised who was behind it.

The State will argue that the SCA extends the sentence to the imposed minimum 15-years for murder.
The Defence will argue that the six-year sentence stays unchanged.



A year after the Supreme Court of Appeal granted the State leave to appeal the six year sence

Further information:
THINGS THAT HAVE CHANGED SINCE JUDGE MASIPA RE-SENTENCED OSCAR TO SIX-YEARS IMPRISONMENT ON MURDER IN JULY 2016 & THE SCA GRANTED THE STATE LEAVE TO APPEAL AGAINST THIS SENTENCE - APPLICATION GRANTED IN NOV 2016:

- In July, Oscar has served one year of his six-year imprisonment. If things stay unchanged and as it currently is, he has to serve another two years before he can apply for parole
- Pistorius was transferred from the Kgosi Mampuru II prison where he was held in a single cell in the hospital section of the prison, to the Atteridgeville Correctional Centre, which is better suited for inmates with disabilities
- In June, he was admitted to hospital for an overnight stay after he allegedly experienced chest pain and shortness of breath. The Department of Correctional Services Spokesperson, Logan Maistry said that the reasons for Pistorius's hospital visit were confidential.
- In July, Pistorius was granted compassionate leave by the Department to attend his grandmother, Joyce Bekker's funeral.
- On November 11, a movie called "Oscar Pistorius: Blade Runner Killer" will premiere worldwide. It tells the story of Pistorius and how he overcame his disability and his apparent fairy tale relationship with Reeva. The movie tells the story from Reeva and her mother's point of view - looking at events leading up to the killing.

IMPORTANT BACKGROUND INFO ON JUDGE MASIPA'S RE-SENTENCE OF PISTORIUS ON THE CHARGE OF MURDER: JULY 2016

- Judge Masipa said it came as no surprise to her that Pistorius was described as a "broken man" during sentencing arguments in June 2016

- During the reading of the sentence in July last year, Oscar seemed emotionless in comparison with a visibly distraught man during sentencing proceedings in June 2016

- Judge Masipa: "The determination of an appropriate sentence that satisfies every relevant interest is never easy. it is made even more difficult by the fact that nothing this court will do ir say today shall being back the life of the deceased. The life of the accused shall also never be the same. He is a hallen hero, who has lost his career, and is ruined financially. The worst is that having taken the life of a fellow human being in the manner that he did, he cannot be at peace. Reeva Steenkamp is gone forever."

- As aggravating factors, Judge Masipa echoed the findings of the Appeal Court when it overturned Pistorius's verdict from culpable homicide to murder: "The accused used a lethal weapon and fired not one, but four shots into the toilet door, knowing full-well that there was someone behind the door. The toilet was a small cubicle and there was no room for escape for the person behind the door. The accused had been trained in the use of and in the handling of firearms. He used a firearms without taking the precaution of firing a warning shot."

- As mitigating factors, she cited Pistorius's belief that there was an intruder in his house, his vulnerability on his stumps, his attempt to save Reeva's life, his remorse and the public's perception of what happened: "It is my view that it must be one of the most difficult things for any accused to have to face the victims of his crime and to apologise. It is highly improbable therefore that the accused would persist in his request to meet the parents of the deceased and ask for forgiveness if he was not genuinely remorseful."

- In aggravation of sentence, the State called Reeva's father, Barry Steenkamp. Trembling on the stand, he described how his daughter's death has devastated the family and that despite Oscar's offers to meet with them, they weren't yet ready.

- Judge Masipa also considered public perception a mitigating factor in this trial, in other words she accepted the view that some in society continued to willfully misrepresent the facts presented in the trial and for that reason continued to believe, wrongly so, that Oscar marched down the passage with evil intent.

- Judge Masipa: "It was the court's duty to impose an appropriate and fair sentence - fearlessly, even if the sentence did not satisfy the public. Punishment is not what you choose to do, it is something that is imposed on you. By it's very nature, punishment is unpleasant, it is uncomfortable, it is painful and it is inconvenient. It is certainly not what you love to do."

IMPORTANT BACKGROUND INFO ABOUT THE SCA'S JUDGMENT IN OVERTURNING THE VERDICT FROM CULPABLE HOMICIDE TO MURDER: DECEMBER 2015

- Justice Eric Leach, reading the ruling on behalf of a five-judge bench unanimous in its verdict, said: “As a result of the errors of law … and on a proper appraisal of the facts, [Pistorius] ought to have been convicted not of culpable homicide on that count but of murder. In the interests of justice the conviction and the sentence imposed in respect thereof must be set aside and the conviction substituted with a conviction of the correct offence.”

- Justice Leach: "This case involves the human tragedy of Shakespearean proportions. The young man overcomes huge physical disabilities to reach Olympian heights as an athlete. He meets a young woman of great natural beauty and a successful model. All is destroyed when he takes her life. The court found the accused to have been a very poor witness. One does really not know what his explanation is having fired the fatal shots. I have no doubt that in firing the fatal shots the accused must have foreseen and therefore did foresee that whoever was behind the toilet door, might die, but reconciled himself to that event occurring and gambled with that person's life. He ought to have been convicted not of culpable homicide on that count, but of murder."

- The issue before the court was whether in shooting Reeva, Pistorius committed the crime of murder, defined as the intentional killing of a human being, or the lesser offence of culpable homicide, defined as the negligent killing of another.

- The judges said Pistorius’s evidence and explanations for killing Steenkamp were implausible and that he had never offered an acceptable explanation for firing four times through a closed door.

- They said Pistorius’s claim – one of several put forward by the defence – of putative private defence, or self-defence in fear of his life, was not rational. His evidence was so contradictory that it was impossible to know his true reason for firing, but it was clear that the person behind the door did not pose any immediate threat to him.

- STATE'S CASE: State prosecutors, arguing during appeal proceedings in November 2015, said that trial judge, Thokozile Masipa, was wrong when she found Pistorius not guilty of murder.

- Chief prosecutor Gerrie Nel argued that Judge Masipa had erred in her application of the legal principle of dolus eventualis, and that she was wrong to conclude that Pistorius had not foreseen that firing four shots into a locked door was likely to kill or injure the person behind it.

- Nel argued that even if Pistorius believed Steenkamp was in bed, there was a criminal intent to bring about the demise of whoever was inside the toilet cubicle.

THE CASE ABOUT DOLUS EVENTUALIS

- Dolus eventualis hinges on whether an accused did foresee the outcome of his actions, rather than whether they should have.

- In this case, Judge Masipa originally accepted Pistorius’s argument that he did not think his actions would lead to the death of the person behind the door. But she found him guilty of culpable homicide after deciding that a reasonable person should have foreseen such an outcome.

- The appeal court judges said Masipa made an error when reaching this verdict. They said the judge was wrong in her application of dolus eventualis, as Pistorius “must have foreseen” that firing into the door could cause the death of whoever was behind it.

- The SCA Justices ruled that Judge Masipa also wrongly conflated the test of dolus eventualis with dolus directus in accepting the defence argument that because Pistorius did not know the person behind the door was Steenkamp meant he could not be guilty of murder.

- While Judge Masipa’s verdict was premised upon an acceptance that Pistorius did not think Steenkamp was in the toilet, the judges said the key thing is that the perpetrator knows his actions could kill that person, regardless of who it is.

- The SCA Judges said the failure to take into account all the evidence – in particular key ballistics evidence – amounted to a failure in law.

- The state further alleged that the trial judge was wrong to dismiss circumstantial evidence that it said proved the accused’s version of events to be impossible.

SCA JUDGES RULE CHANGE OF VERDICT DOES NOT SPEAK TO JUDGE MASIPA PERSONALLY

- While the appeal court ruled that Judge Masipa had made several errors of law, it also commended her role in the trial. Justice Leach said: “Before closing, it is necessary to make a final comment. The trial was conducted in the glare of international attention and the focus of television cameras, which must have added to the inherently heavy rigours that are brought to bear upon trial courts in conducting lengthy and complicated trials. The trial judge conducted the hearing with a degree of dignity and patience that is a credit to the judiciary. The fact that this court has determined that certain mistakes were made should not be seen as an adverse comment upon her competence and ability. The fact is that different judges reach different conclusions and, in the light of an appeal structure, those of the appellate court prevail. But the fact that the appeal has succeeded is not to be regarded as a slight upon the trial judge who is to be congratulated for the manner in which she conducted the proceedings.”

Press Release:


Oscar Pistorius: State Sentence Appeal
Last year, convicted murderer Oscar Pistorius was sentenced to six years in prison for killing his
girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp – a sentence the State called "shockingly lenient". Now the State is
heading back to Bloemfontein to argue that the Justices of the Supreme Court of Appeal should
increase Pistorius' sentence to the prescribed minimum sentence for murder – 15 years. Carte
Blanche asks: can the State succeed in its attempt to extend Pistorius’ time behind bars?

Script:


OSCAR SENTENCE APPEAL
PRODUCERS: Este de Klerk & Anna-Maria van Niekerk
PRESENTER: John Webb
TX DATE: 5 November 2017


PROMOS:

PROMO 1: 15 seconds

ACTING APPEAL COURT JUSTICE PIETER MEYER: WHY SHOOTING FOUR SHOTS AT INTRUDER THROUGH THE DOOR?

JOHN LINK: The Oscar Pistorius case was back in court this week as the state appealed his 6-year sentence for murder -- the crux of their argument? That that sentence was shockingly inappropriate.

PROMO 2: 15 seconds

It’s State vs Oscar Pistorius in the Supreme Court of Appeal again.

ADV. ANDREA JOHNSON: HE SHOULD HAVE TAKEN CONFIDENCE OF THE COURT AND SAID THIS IS WHY I DID IT...

ADV. BARRY ROUX: I CANNOT STAND HERE IN VIEW OF THE CONVICTION AND JUSTIFY THE FOUR SHOTS.

INSERT:

JOHN LINK: It’s been two years to the day since we stood at this exact spot at the Bloemfontein Supreme Court of Appeal, after the State successfully appealed Oscar Pistorius’ 2014 conviction of culpable homicide -- having it overturned to murder. He’d killed girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp in the early hours of Valentine’s Day, 2013. He’s maintained throughout that he’d mistaken her for an intruder.

In his judgment overturning the conviction to murder, Appeal court Justice Eric Leach called it a tragedy of Shakespearean proportions.

[3 DECEMBER 2015/SUPREME COURT OF APPEAL] APPEAL COURT JUSTICE ERIC LEACH: A young man overcomes huge physical disabilities to reach Olympian heights as an athlete. He meets a young woman of great natural beauty and a successful model. All is destroyed when he takes her life. The court found the accused to have been a very poor witness. One does really not know what his explanation is having fired the fatal shots.

Judge Thokozile Masipa imposed a six-year sentence for the charge of murder, despite the fact that a prescribed minimum sentence is 15 years -- unless there are substantial and compelling circumstances.

[6 JULY 2016/TRIAL JUDGE THOKOZILE MASIPA] It’s the court’s duty to impose an appropriate and fair sentence - fearlessly, even if the sentence did not satisfy the public.
JOHN LINK: The state argues that she wrongly emphasised the mitigating factors, displaying “maudlin sympathy” for Oscar Pistorius.

Mitigating factors Judge Masipa found substantial and compelling, included Pistorius’ belief that there was an intruder in his house, his vulnerability on his stumps, his attempt to save Reeva’s life, that he bargained with God to save her and his remorse, illustrated by wanting to meet with her parents.

JOHN LINK: The state has argued that the sentence handed down by Judge Masipa is shockingly inappropriate -- but more than that they say that in arriving at that figure, the Judge committed a material misdirection.

Since their last court appearance, chief State Prosecutor, advocate Gerrie Nel has left the NPA. Advocate Andrea Johnson argued for the State before presiding officer, Justice Lebotsang Bosielo, Appeal Court Justice Willie Seriti and three acting Appeal Justices Pieter Meyer, Colin Lamont and Fikile Mokgohloa.
For advocate Johnson, this was not only about having Pistorius’ sentence increased, but also to correct a legal principle.

ADV. ANDREA JOHNSON: OUR POSITION IS AS FOLLOWS -- THERE ARE NO COMPELLING AND SUBSTANTIAL REASONS WHICH JUSTIFY LESSER SENTENCE. THE COURT A QUO MATERIALLY MISDIRECTED ITSELF IN FINDING THAT THERE ARE. THE STARTING POINT IS MINIMUM SENTENCE OF 15 YEARS IMPRISONMENT.

In court, the STATE emphasised that the sentence was inappropriately lenient, due to “material misdirections” on (bullet points) *his physical disability; *foreseeability; *rehabilitation; *remorse vs. regret and having *no acceptable explanation.

The DEFENCE focused on Pistorius’ (bullet points) *emotional & physical vulnerability; *his state of mind; *his belief that there was an intruder in his home; *being a broken man; and *a lack of intention to kill Steenkamp.

RETIRED JUDGE JOOS HEFER: There are no reasons in the trial court judgment for the duration of the prison sentence.

Retired Judge Joos Hefer served 19 of his 27 years on the bench as an Appeal Court Justice.

RETIRED JUDGE JOOS HEFER: But eventually she came down hard on the side of the mitigating circumstances forgetting the seriousness the offence.

ADV. ANDREA JOHNSON: THE COURT A QUO OUGHT TO HAVE STARTED, LISTED FIRST LISTED THE SUBSTANTIVE AND COMPELLING, THEN SAID BECAUSE OF THEIR PRESENCE, I NOW DEVIATE FROM THE MINIMUM SENTENCES...BUT THE COURT DOES NOT HAVE A CLEAN SLATE.

RETIRED JUDGE JOOS HEFER: You have to weigh circumstances counting against the accused, against those who count in his favour. And if you don’t list them, if you merely talk about what kind of man he was and what kind of deed he...and what kind of act he committed, then it’s difficult to see how the judge really weighed up and came to the conclusion as the legislation requires.

Retired Free State High Court Judge Fred Beckley.

RETIRED JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: This is crime which is referred to in the legislation which required a minimum of 15 years imprisonment unless there are compelling circumstances. That’s your starting point...the mitigating factors play second fiddle. You look at the retribution and deterrent effects first and then only after that do you look at for instance rehabilitation.

ADV. ANDREA JOHNSON: WHAT PERHAPS MAKES THE CRIME MORE REPREHENSIBLE IS THAT KILLING WAS SENSELESS AND GRATUITOUS. NO ACCEPTABLE REASON HAS BEEN ADVANCED BY THE RESPONDENT ON WHY HE KILLED THE DECEASED.

JOHN LINK: The justices kept coming back to the idea that because there’s no explanation as to why he fired the four shots, there could not be any remorse.

APPEAL COURT JUSTICE LEBOTSANG BOSIELO: HE MADE VARIOUS ATTEMPTS TO TALK TO FAMILY, APOLOGISED PUBLICLY IN COURT...WHAT MORE COULD HE HAVE DONE?

ADV. ANDREA JOHNSON: HE SHOULD HAVE TAKEN CONFIDENCE OF THE COURT AND SAID THIS IS WHY I DID IT...IT IS INCONCEIVABLE A RATIONAL PERSON COULD HAVE BELIEVED HE WAS ENTITLED TO FIRE AT THIS PERSON WITH HEAVY CALIBRE FIREARM WITHOUT TAKING EVEN THAT MOST ELEMENTARY PRECAUTION OF FIRING A WARNING.

Defence advocate Barry Roux focused on Pistorius’ physical and emotional identity while the Justices repeatedly returned to the burning unanswered question:

ACTING APPEAL COURT JUSTICE PIETER MEYER: WHY SHOOTING FOUR SHOTS AT THE INTRUDER?

ADV BARRY ROUX: I CANNOT STAND HERE IN VIEW OF THE CONVICTION AND JUSTIFY THE FOUR SHOTS...HE WAS JUST FIRING, IT WAS NOT FIRING WITH THAT EVIL INTENT…HIS VIEW IS I AM BLAMED THAT I WANTED TO KILL MISS STEENKAMP AND I DID, BUT THAT WAS AN ACCIDENT, I NEVER WANTED TO KILL HER.

JOHN LINK: Barry Roux made the point that it would be a mistake to see this purely as a 6-year sentence because you need to take into consideration the one year Oscar has already spent behind bars as well as his house arrest - this is in fact effectively an 8-year sentence.

ADV. BARRY ROUX: IN THE PROCESS OF FIRING THE FOUR SHOTS...HE KILLED SOMEONE HE DID NOT WANT TO KILL.

ACTING APPEAL COURT JUSTICE PIETER MEYER: WAS HE THEN PREPARED TO KILL AN INTRUDER?

ADV. BARRY ROUX: I THINK MANY PEOPLE ARE UNFORTUNATELY PREPARED TO KILL INTRUDERS IF THERE IS A PROBLEM.

ACTING APPEAL COURT COLIN LAMONT: THEN HIS REMORSE ARGUMENT FALLS AWAY...IF HIS INTENTION WAS TO KILL PERSON INSIDE.

ADV. BARRY ROUX: HOW CAN YOU HAVE REMORSE AGAINST INTRUDER WHO IS NOT REAL AT THE END? AND HIS REMORSE MUST INEVITABLY BE FOCUSED ON MISS STEENKAMP.

JUDGE JOOS HEFER: I think Barry...made exactly the same mistake that the trial judge made -- trying to hold his client up as a pitiable person...forgetting that in the context of the legislation, that has already been said to merge into nothing really when it comes to deciding whether are that required sentences.

JOHN LINK: Power to sentence rests with the trial court so it’s not a foregone conclusion that the SCA will intervene, however Andrea Johnson argued that because of the material misdirections the trial court has committed, the SCA is “duty bound” to intervene.

RETIRED JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: A court of appeal must find that there was a misdirection which was relevant and then of course they have the discretion to intervene.

Judgment was reserved. If the NPA’s appeal does not succeed, Pistorius could conceivably apply for parole soon.

JOHN: It’s an important case to provide clarity on minimum sentences and how much leeway judges have to deviate?

BECKLEY: The norm has not been laid down in any authoritative decision. I sincerely hope that the judgment will be an unanimous one -- of the five judges on the bench -- and that they will lay down the law.

It is the State's second appeal against the findings by Trial Judge Thokozila Masipa: first the successful appeal against the verdict of culpable homicide - overturned by the SCA in a unanimous judgment of a full bench of judges - to murder; and the State's second appeal against the six-year sentence Judge Masipa imposed on Pistorius for murder. The State will argue that the former athlete's sentence is "shockingly inappropriate for the crime of murder". The NPA will argue that Pistorius should have been handed the minimum term of 15 years behind bars. NPA spokesperson, Luvuyo Mfaku, said: "The State, in the papers, we stipulate that the sentence imposed is shockingly low. The presiding officer has the discretion to deviate from the minimum prescribed sentence when compelling and substantiate circumstances exist. But... with this matter, the presiding officer exercised that discretion in a very lenient manner." Pistorius's defence team lead by defence advocate Barry Roux, has always argued that Pistorius did not deliberately kill Reeva Steenkamp. Pistorius has always insisted the shooting was a mistake, saying he thought an intruder had entered his home and he feared for his safety. He fired four shots through a locked toilet door, hitting Reeva in the head, arm and hip. During his trial in 2014, Pistorius testified in court it was only when he battered down the door with a cricket bat that he realised who was behind it. The State will argue that the SCA extends the sentence to the imposed minimum 15-years for murder. The Defence will argue that the six-year sentence stays unchanged. A year after the Supreme Court of Appeal granted the State leave to appeal the six year sence Further information: THINGS THAT HAVE CHANGED SINCE JUDGE MASIPA RE-SENTENCED OSCAR TO SIX-YEARS IMPRISONMENT ON MURDER IN JULY 2016 & THE SCA GRANTED THE STATE LEAVE TO APPEAL AGAINST THIS SENTENCE - APPLICATION GRANTED IN NOV 2016: - In July, Oscar has served one year of his six-year imprisonment. If things stay unchanged and as it currently is, he has to serve another two years before he can apply for parole - Pistorius was transferred from the Kgosi Mampuru II prison where he was held in a single cell in the hospital section of the prison, to the Atteridgeville Correctional Centre, which is better suited for inmates with disabilities - In June, he was admitted to hospital for an overnight stay after he allegedly experienced chest pain and shortness of breath. The Department of Correctional Services Spokesperson, Logan Maistry said that the reasons for Pistorius's hospital visit were confidential. - In July, Pistorius was granted compassionate leave by the Department to attend his grandmother, Joyce Bekker's funeral. - On November 11, a movie called "Oscar Pistorius: Blade Runner Killer" will premiere worldwide. It tells the story of Pistorius and how he overcame his disability and his apparent fairy tale relationship with Reeva. The movie tells the story from Reeva and her mother's point of view - looking at events leading up to the killing. IMPORTANT BACKGROUND INFO ON JUDGE MASIPA'S RE-SENTENCE OF PISTORIUS ON THE CHARGE OF MURDER: JULY 2016 - Judge Masipa said it came as no surprise to her that Pistorius was described as a "broken man" during sentencing arguments in June 2016 - During the reading of the sentence in July last year, Oscar seemed emotionless in comparison with a visibly distraught man during sentencing proceedings in June 2016 - Judge Masipa: "The determination of an appropriate sentence that satisfies every relevant interest is never easy. it is made even more difficult by the fact that nothing this court will do ir say today shall being back the life of the deceased. The life of the accused shall also never be the same. He is a hallen hero, who has lost his career, and is ruined financially. The worst is that having taken the life of a fellow human being in the manner that he did, he cannot be at peace. Reeva Steenkamp is gone forever." - As aggravating factors, Judge Masipa echoed the findings of the Appeal Court when it overturned Pistorius's verdict from culpable homicide to murder: "The accused used a lethal weapon and fired not one, but four shots into the toilet door, knowing full-well that there was someone behind the door. The toilet was a small cubicle and there was no room for escape for the person behind the door. The accused had been trained in the use of and in the handling of firearms. He used a firearms without taking the precaution of firing a warning shot." - As mitigating factors, she cited Pistorius's belief that there was an intruder in his house, his vulnerability on his stumps, his attempt to save Reeva's life, his remorse and the public's perception of what happened: "It is my view that it must be one of the most difficult things for any accused to have to face the victims of his crime and to apologise. It is highly improbable therefore that the accused would persist in his request to meet the parents of the deceased and ask for forgiveness if he was not genuinely remorseful." - In aggravation of sentence, the State called Reeva's father, Barry Steenkamp. Trembling on the stand, he described how his daughter's death has devastated the family and that despite Oscar's offers to meet with them, they weren't yet ready. - Judge Masipa also considered public perception a mitigating factor in this trial, in other words she accepted the view that some in society continued to willfully misrepresent the facts presented in the trial and for that reason continued to believe, wrongly so, that Oscar marched down the passage with evil intent. - Judge Masipa: "It was the court's duty to impose an appropriate and fair sentence - fearlessly, even if the sentence did not satisfy the public. Punishment is not what you choose to do, it is something that is imposed on you. By it's very nature, punishment is unpleasant, it is uncomfortable, it is painful and it is inconvenient. It is certainly not what you love to do." IMPORTANT BACKGROUND INFO ABOUT THE SCA'S JUDGMENT IN OVERTURNING THE VERDICT FROM CULPABLE HOMICIDE TO MURDER: DECEMBER 2015 - Justice Eric Leach, reading the ruling on behalf of a five-judge bench unanimous in its verdict, said: “As a result of the errors of law … and on a proper appraisal of the facts, [Pistorius] ought to have been convicted not of culpable homicide on that count but of murder. In the interests of justice the conviction and the sentence imposed in respect thereof must be set aside and the conviction substituted with a conviction of the correct offence.” - Justice Leach: "This case involves the human tragedy of Shakespearean proportions. The young man overcomes huge physical disabilities to reach Olympian heights as an athlete. He meets a young woman of great natural beauty and a successful model. All is destroyed when he takes her life. The court found the accused to have been a very poor witness. One does really not know what his explanation is having fired the fatal shots. I have no doubt that in firing the fatal shots the accused must have foreseen and therefore did foresee that whoever was behind the toilet door, might die, but reconciled himself to that event occurring and gambled with that person's life. He ought to have been convicted not of culpable homicide on that count, but of murder." - The issue before the court was whether in shooting Reeva, Pistorius committed the crime of murder, defined as the intentional killing of a human being, or the lesser offence of culpable homicide, defined as the negligent killing of another. - The judges said Pistorius’s evidence and explanations for killing Steenkamp were implausible and that he had never offered an acceptable explanation for firing four times through a closed door. - They said Pistorius’s claim – one of several put forward by the defence – of putative private defence, or self-defence in fear of his life, was not rational. His evidence was so contradictory that it was impossible to know his true reason for firing, but it was clear that the person behind the door did not pose any immediate threat to him. - STATE'S CASE: State prosecutors, arguing during appeal proceedings in November 2015, said that trial judge, Thokozile Masipa, was wrong when she found Pistorius not guilty of murder. - Chief prosecutor Gerrie Nel argued that Judge Masipa had erred in her application of the legal principle of dolus eventualis, and that she was wrong to conclude that Pistorius had not foreseen that firing four shots into a locked door was likely to kill or injure the person behind it. - Nel argued that even if Pistorius believed Steenkamp was in bed, there was a criminal intent to bring about the demise of whoever was inside the toilet cubicle. THE CASE ABOUT DOLUS EVENTUALIS - Dolus eventualis hinges on whether an accused did foresee the outcome of his actions, rather than whether they should have. - In this case, Judge Masipa originally accepted Pistorius’s argument that he did not think his actions would lead to the death of the person behind the door. But she found him guilty of culpable homicide after deciding that a reasonable person should have foreseen such an outcome. - The appeal court judges said Masipa made an error when reaching this verdict. They said the judge was wrong in her application of dolus eventualis, as Pistorius “must have foreseen” that firing into the door could cause the death of whoever was behind it. - The SCA Justices ruled that Judge Masipa also wrongly conflated the test of dolus eventualis with dolus directus in accepting the defence argument that because Pistorius did not know the person behind the door was Steenkamp meant he could not be guilty of murder. - While Judge Masipa’s verdict was premised upon an acceptance that Pistorius did not think Steenkamp was in the toilet, the judges said the key thing is that the perpetrator knows his actions could kill that person, regardless of who it is. - The SCA Judges said the failure to take into account all the evidence – in particular key ballistics evidence – amounted to a failure in law. - The state further alleged that the trial judge was wrong to dismiss circumstantial evidence that it said proved the accused’s version of events to be impossible. SCA JUDGES RULE CHANGE OF VERDICT DOES NOT SPEAK TO JUDGE MASIPA PERSONALLY - While the appeal court ruled that Judge Masipa had made several errors of law, it also commended her role in the trial. Justice Leach said: “Before closing, it is necessary to make a final comment. The trial was conducted in the glare of international attention and the focus of television cameras, which must have added to the inherently heavy rigours that are brought to bear upon trial courts in conducting lengthy and complicated trials. The trial judge conducted the hearing with a degree of dignity and patience that is a credit to the judiciary. The fact that this court has determined that certain mistakes were made should not be seen as an adverse comment upon her competence and ability. The fact is that different judges reach different conclusions and, in the light of an appeal structure, those of the appellate court prevail. But the fact that the appeal has succeeded is not to be regarded as a slight upon the trial judge who is to be congratulated for the manner in which she conducted the proceedings.” Extra Budget Items: 2017 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 24 November 2017 Press Release: Oscar Pistorius: State Sentence Appeal Last year, convicted murderer Oscar Pistorius was sentenced to six years in prison for killing his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp – a sentence the State called "shockingly lenient". Now the State is heading back to Bloemfontein to argue that the Justices of the Supreme Court of Appeal should increase Pistorius' sentence to the prescribed minimum sentence for murder – 15 years. Carte Blanche asks: can the State succeed in its attempt to extend Pistorius’ time behind bars? Script: OSCAR SENTENCE APPEAL PRODUCERS: Este de Klerk & Anna-Maria van Niekerk PRESENTER: John Webb TX DATE: 5 November 2017 PROMOS: PROMO 1: 15 seconds ACTING APPEAL COURT JUSTICE PIETER MEYER: WHY SHOOTING FOUR SHOTS AT INTRUDER THROUGH THE DOOR? JOHN LINK: The Oscar Pistorius case was back in court this week as the state appealed his 6-year sentence for murder -- the crux of their argument? That that sentence was shockingly inappropriate. PROMO 2: 15 seconds It’s State vs Oscar Pistorius in the Supreme Court of Appeal again. ADV. ANDREA JOHNSON: HE SHOULD HAVE TAKEN CONFIDENCE OF THE COURT AND SAID THIS IS WHY I DID IT... ADV. BARRY ROUX: I CANNOT STAND HERE IN VIEW OF THE CONVICTION AND JUSTIFY THE FOUR SHOTS. INSERT: JOHN LINK: It’s been two years to the day since we stood at this exact spot at the Bloemfontein Supreme Court of Appeal, after the State successfully appealed Oscar Pistorius’ 2014 conviction of culpable homicide -- having it overturned to murder. He’d killed girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp in the early hours of Valentine’s Day, 2013. He’s maintained throughout that he’d mistaken her for an intruder. In his judgment overturning the conviction to murder, Appeal court Justice Eric Leach called it a tragedy of Shakespearean proportions. [3 DECEMBER 2015/SUPREME COURT OF APPEAL] APPEAL COURT JUSTICE ERIC LEACH: A young man overcomes huge physical disabilities to reach Olympian heights as an athlete. He meets a young woman of great natural beauty and a successful model. All is destroyed when he takes her life. The court found the accused to have been a very poor witness. One does really not know what his explanation is having fired the fatal shots. Judge Thokozile Masipa imposed a six-year sentence for the charge of murder, despite the fact that a prescribed minimum sentence is 15 years -- unless there are substantial and compelling circumstances. [6 JULY 2016/TRIAL JUDGE THOKOZILE MASIPA] It’s the court’s duty to impose an appropriate and fair sentence - fearlessly, even if the sentence did not satisfy the public. JOHN LINK: The state argues that she wrongly emphasised the mitigating factors, displaying “maudlin sympathy” for Oscar Pistorius. Mitigating factors Judge Masipa found substantial and compelling, included Pistorius’ belief that there was an intruder in his house, his vulnerability on his stumps, his attempt to save Reeva’s life, that he bargained with God to save her and his remorse, illustrated by wanting to meet with her parents. JOHN LINK: The state has argued that the sentence handed down by Judge Masipa is shockingly inappropriate -- but more than that they say that in arriving at that figure, the Judge committed a material misdirection. Since their last court appearance, chief State Prosecutor, advocate Gerrie Nel has left the NPA. Advocate Andrea Johnson argued for the State before presiding officer, Justice Lebotsang Bosielo, Appeal Court Justice Willie Seriti and three acting Appeal Justices Pieter Meyer, Colin Lamont and Fikile Mokgohloa. For advocate Johnson, this was not only about having Pistorius’ sentence increased, but also to correct a legal principle. ADV. ANDREA JOHNSON: OUR POSITION IS AS FOLLOWS -- THERE ARE NO COMPELLING AND SUBSTANTIAL REASONS WHICH JUSTIFY LESSER SENTENCE. THE COURT A QUO MATERIALLY MISDIRECTED ITSELF IN FINDING THAT THERE ARE. THE STARTING POINT IS MINIMUM SENTENCE OF 15 YEARS IMPRISONMENT. In court, the STATE emphasised that the sentence was inappropriately lenient, due to “material misdirections” on (bullet points) *his physical disability; *foreseeability; *rehabilitation; *remorse vs. regret and having *no acceptable explanation. The DEFENCE focused on Pistorius’ (bullet points) *emotional & physical vulnerability; *his state of mind; *his belief that there was an intruder in his home; *being a broken man; and *a lack of intention to kill Steenkamp. RETIRED JUDGE JOOS HEFER: There are no reasons in the trial court judgment for the duration of the prison sentence. Retired Judge Joos Hefer served 19 of his 27 years on the bench as an Appeal Court Justice. RETIRED JUDGE JOOS HEFER: But eventually she came down hard on the side of the mitigating circumstances forgetting the seriousness the offence. ADV. ANDREA JOHNSON: THE COURT A QUO OUGHT TO HAVE STARTED, LISTED FIRST LISTED THE SUBSTANTIVE AND COMPELLING, THEN SAID BECAUSE OF THEIR PRESENCE, I NOW DEVIATE FROM THE MINIMUM SENTENCES...BUT THE COURT DOES NOT HAVE A CLEAN SLATE. RETIRED JUDGE JOOS HEFER: You have to weigh circumstances counting against the accused, against those who count in his favour. And if you don’t list them, if you merely talk about what kind of man he was and what kind of deed he...and what kind of act he committed, then it’s difficult to see how the judge really weighed up and came to the conclusion as the legislation requires. Retired Free State High Court Judge Fred Beckley. RETIRED JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: This is crime which is referred to in the legislation which required a minimum of 15 years imprisonment unless there are compelling circumstances. That’s your starting point...the mitigating factors play second fiddle. You look at the retribution and deterrent effects first and then only after that do you look at for instance rehabilitation. ADV. ANDREA JOHNSON: WHAT PERHAPS MAKES THE CRIME MORE REPREHENSIBLE IS THAT KILLING WAS SENSELESS AND GRATUITOUS. NO ACCEPTABLE REASON HAS BEEN ADVANCED BY THE RESPONDENT ON WHY HE KILLED THE DECEASED. JOHN LINK: The justices kept coming back to the idea that because there’s no explanation as to why he fired the four shots, there could not be any remorse. APPEAL COURT JUSTICE LEBOTSANG BOSIELO: HE MADE VARIOUS ATTEMPTS TO TALK TO FAMILY, APOLOGISED PUBLICLY IN COURT...WHAT MORE COULD HE HAVE DONE? ADV. ANDREA JOHNSON: HE SHOULD HAVE TAKEN CONFIDENCE OF THE COURT AND SAID THIS IS WHY I DID IT...IT IS INCONCEIVABLE A RATIONAL PERSON COULD HAVE BELIEVED HE WAS ENTITLED TO FIRE AT THIS PERSON WITH HEAVY CALIBRE FIREARM WITHOUT TAKING EVEN THAT MOST ELEMENTARY PRECAUTION OF FIRING A WARNING. Defence advocate Barry Roux focused on Pistorius’ physical and emotional identity while the Justices repeatedly returned to the burning unanswered question: ACTING APPEAL COURT JUSTICE PIETER MEYER: WHY SHOOTING FOUR SHOTS AT THE INTRUDER? ADV BARRY ROUX: I CANNOT STAND HERE IN VIEW OF THE CONVICTION AND JUSTIFY THE FOUR SHOTS...HE WAS JUST FIRING, IT WAS NOT FIRING WITH THAT EVIL INTENT…HIS VIEW IS I AM BLAMED THAT I WANTED TO KILL MISS STEENKAMP AND I DID, BUT THAT WAS AN ACCIDENT, I NEVER WANTED TO KILL HER. JOHN LINK: Barry Roux made the point that it would be a mistake to see this purely as a 6-year sentence because you need to take into consideration the one year Oscar has already spent behind bars as well as his house arrest - this is in fact effectively an 8-year sentence. ADV. BARRY ROUX: IN THE PROCESS OF FIRING THE FOUR SHOTS...HE KILLED SOMEONE HE DID NOT WANT TO KILL. ACTING APPEAL COURT JUSTICE PIETER MEYER: WAS HE THEN PREPARED TO KILL AN INTRUDER? ADV. BARRY ROUX: I THINK MANY PEOPLE ARE UNFORTUNATELY PREPARED TO KILL INTRUDERS IF THERE IS A PROBLEM. ACTING APPEAL COURT COLIN LAMONT: THEN HIS REMORSE ARGUMENT FALLS AWAY...IF HIS INTENTION WAS TO KILL PERSON INSIDE. ADV. BARRY ROUX: HOW CAN YOU HAVE REMORSE AGAINST INTRUDER WHO IS NOT REAL AT THE END? AND HIS REMORSE MUST INEVITABLY BE FOCUSED ON MISS STEENKAMP. JUDGE JOOS HEFER: I think Barry...made exactly the same mistake that the trial judge made -- trying to hold his client up as a pitiable person...forgetting that in the context of the legislation, that has already been said to merge into nothing really when it comes to deciding whether are that required sentences. JOHN LINK: Power to sentence rests with the trial court so it’s not a foregone conclusion that the SCA will intervene, however Andrea Johnson argued that because of the material misdirections the trial court has committed, the SCA is “duty bound” to intervene. RETIRED JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: A court of appeal must find that there was a misdirection which was relevant and then of course they have the discretion to intervene. Judgment was reserved. If the NPA’s appeal does not succeed, Pistorius could conceivably apply for parole soon. JOHN: It’s an important case to provide clarity on minimum sentences and how much leeway judges have to deviate? BECKLEY: The norm has not been laid down in any authoritative decision. I sincerely hope that the judgment will be an unanimous one -- of the five judges on the bench -- and that they will lay down the law. [ENDS]

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Just more than a year and four months since Oscar Pistorius was sentenced to six years in prison for murder, his future hangs in the balance again.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In December 2015, Supreme Court of Appeal Justice Eric Leach, who wrote and read the ruling on behalf of a five-judge bench unanimous in its verdict, opened the verdict with the following words: "This case involves the human tragedy of Shakespearean proportions. The young man overcomes huge physical disabilities to reach Olympian heights as an athlete. He meets a young woman of great natural beauty and a successful model. All is destroyed when he takes her life. The court found the accused to have been a very poor witness. One does really not know what his explanation is having fired the fatal shots. I have no doubt that in firing the fatal shots the accused must have foreseen and therefore did foresee that whoever was behind the toilet door, might die, but reconciled himself to that event occurring and gambled with that person's life. He ought to have been convicted not of culpable homicide on that count, but of murder." It is perhaps upon these words, that the NPA and the trial's chief state prosecutor, adv Gerrie Nel, said the sentence that Pretoria High Court Trial Judge, Thokozile Masipa, imposed on Oscar Pistorius on the charge of murder, is "shockingly inappropriate". And this is what the State will build its case on and argue in the Appeal Court in Bloemfontein on the 3rd of November. In July 2016, when Judge Masipa sentenced Pistorius for a second time, she sentenced him to six years imprisonment for the murder of Reeva Steenkamp, saying the mitigating factors outweighed the aggravating factors and therefore the prescribed 15-year minimum sentence for murder would be unjust. At the time, adv Nel said the sentence was too lenient and that the State would appeal it. In August 2016, Judge Masipa dismissed the State's application for leave to appeal the sentence she imposed on Oscar. In dismissing the application, Judge Masipa said she was not persuaded that there was a reasonable prospect of success at another court. Adv Nel then launched an application directly at the SCA, and in November last year the court ruled that the State and Defence would have to give oral arguments in the State's appeal against Oscar's sentence. These are the arguments that will be heard on the 3rd of November in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein - and this appeal, once again, let Oscar Pistorius's future lies in the balance: another chapter of a protracted trial that has sustained global attention.

The toilet was a small cubicle and there was no room for escape for the person behind the door. The accused had been trained in the use of and in the handling of firearms. He used a firearms without taking the precaution of firing a warning shot." - As mitigating factors, she cited Pistorius's belief that there was an intruder in his house, his vulnerability on his stumps, his attempt to save Reeva's life, his remorse and the public's perception of what happened: "It is my view that it must be one of the most difficult things for any accused to have to face the victims of his crime and to apologise. It is highly improbable therefore that the accused would persist in his request to meet the parents of the deceased and ask for forgiveness if he was not genuinely remorseful." - In aggravation of sentence, the State called Reeva's father, Barry Steenkamp. Trembling on the stand, he described how his daughter's death has devastated the family and that despite Oscar's offers to meet with them, they weren't yet ready. - Judge Masipa also considered public perception a mitigating factor in this trial, in other words she accepted the view that some in society continued to willfully misrepresent the facts presented in the trial and for that reason continued to believe, wrongly so, that Oscar marched down the passage with evil intent. - Judge Masipa: "It was the court's duty to impose an appropriate and fair sentence - fearlessly, even if the sentence did not satisfy the public. Punishment is not what you choose to do, it is something that is imposed on you. By it's very nature, punishment is unpleasant, it is uncomfortable, it is painful and it is inconvenient. It is certainly not what you love to do." IMPORTANT BACKGROUND INFO ABOUT THE SCA'S JUDGMENT IN OVERTURNING THE VERDICT FROM CULPABLE HOMICIDE TO MURDER: DECEMBER 2015 - Justice Eric Leach, reading the ruling on behalf of a five-judge bench unanimous in its verdict, said: “As a result of the errors of law … and on a proper appraisal of the facts, [Pistorius] ought to have been convicted not of culpable homicide on that count but of murder. In the interests of justice the conviction and the sentence imposed in respect thereof must be set aside and the conviction substituted with a conviction of the correct offence.” - Justice Leach: "This case involves the human tragedy of Shakespearean proportions. The young man overcomes huge physical disabilities to reach Olympian heights as an athlete. He meets a young woman of great natural beauty and a successful model. All is destroyed when he takes her life. The court found the accused to have been a very poor witness. One does really not know what his explanation is having fired the fatal shots. I have no doubt that in firing the fatal shots the accused must have foreseen and therefore did foresee that whoever was behind the toilet door, might die, but reconciled himself to that event occurring and gambled with that person's life. He ought to have been convicted not of culpable homicide on that count, but of murder." - The issue before the court was whether in shooting Reeva, Pistorius committed the crime of murder, defined as the intentional killing of a human being, or the lesser offence of culpable homicide, defined as the negligent killing of another. - The judges said Pistorius’s evidence and explanations for killing Steenkamp were implausible and that he had never offered an acceptable explanation for firing four times through a closed door. - They said Pistorius’s claim – one of several put forward by the defence – of putative private defence, or self-defence in fear of his life, was not rational. His evidence was so contradictory that it was impossible to know his true reason for firing, but it was clear that the person behind the door did not pose any immediate threat to him. - STATE'S CASE: State prosecutors, arguing during appeal proceedings in November 2015, said that trial judge, Thokozile Masipa, was wrong when she found Pistorius not guilty of murder. - Chief prosecutor Gerrie Nel argued that Judge Masipa had erred in her application of the legal principle of dolus eventualis, and that she was wrong to conclude that Pistorius had not foreseen that firing four shots into a locked door was likely to kill or injure the person behind it. - Nel argued that even if Pistorius believed Steenkamp was in bed, there was a criminal intent to bring about the demise of whoever was inside the toilet cubicle. THE CASE ABOUT DOLUS EVENTUALIS - Dolus eventualis hinges on whether an accused did foresee the outcome of his actions, rather than whether they should have. - In this case, Judge Masipa originally accepted Pistorius’s argument that he did not think his actions would lead to the death of the person behind the door. But she found him guilty of culpable homicide after deciding that a reasonable person should have foreseen such an outcome. - The appeal court judges said Masipa made an error when reaching this verdict. They said the judge was wrong in her application of dolus eventualis, as Pistorius “must have foreseen” that firing into the door could cause the death of whoever was behind it. - The SCA Justices ruled that Judge Masipa also wrongly conflated the test of dolus eventualis with dolus directus in accepting the defence argument that because Pistorius did not know the person behind the door was Steenkamp meant he could not be guilty of murder. - While Judge Masipa’s verdict was premised upon an acceptance that Pistorius did not think Steenkamp was in the toilet, the judges said the key thing is that the perpetrator knows his actions could kill that person, regardless of who it is. - The SCA Judges said the failure to take into account all the evidence – in particular key ballistics evidence – amounted to a failure in law. - The state further alleged that the trial judge was wrong to dismiss circumstantial evidence that it said proved the accused’s version of events to be impossible. SCA JUDGES RULE CHANGE OF VERDICT DOES NOT SPEAK TO JUDGE MASIPA PERSONALLY - While the appeal court ruled that Judge Masipa had made several errors of law, it also commended her role in the trial. Justice Leach said: “Before closing, it is necessary to make a final comment. The trial was conducted in the glare of international attention and the focus of television cameras, which must have added to the inherently heavy rigours that are brought to bear upon trial courts in conducting lengthy and complicated trials. The trial judge conducted the hearing with a degree of dignity and patience that is a credit to the judiciary. The fact that this court has determined that certain mistakes were made should not be seen as an adverse comment upon her competence and ability. The fact is that different judges reach different conclusions and, in the light of an appeal structure, those of the appellate court prevail. But the fact that the appeal has succeeded is not to be regarded as a slight upon the trial judge who is to be congratulated for the manner in which she conducted the proceedings.”
